model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Pentago on a standard 6x6 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you, opponent) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - The board is 6x6. - You are given two 6x6 arrays (or array-like objects) containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid (no overlaps): never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Quadrants are 3x3 sub-boards indexed as: - `quad = 0`: rows 1..3, cols 1..3 (top-left). - `quad = 1`: rows 1..3, cols 4..6 (top-right). - `quad = 2`: rows 4..6, cols 1..3 (bottom-left). - `quad = 3`: rows 4..6, cols 4..6 (bottom-right). - A quadrant rotation rotates the chosen 3x3 sub-board in place and affects BOTH players' marbles in that quadrant. - `L` is 90 degrees anticlockwise; `R` is 90 degrees clockwise. - After placement and rotation, a player wins if they have 5 (or more) marbles in a row in any straight line: horizontal, vertical, or diagonal (either diagonal direction). - If both players have a 5-in-a-row after your move is applied, the result is a draw. - If neither player has a 5-in-a-row and the board is full, the result is a draw. # Action / Return Format - Return a single string move formatted exactly as: `"row,col,quad,dir"`. - `row` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `col` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `quad` is 0..3. - `dir` is `L` or `R`. - A legal move must place exactly one of your marbles on an empty cell, then rotate exactly one quadrant 90 degrees in the chosen direction. - Example syntax: `"6,5,2,L"` means place at row 6 col 5, then rotate quadrant 2 left. - You may assume at least one empty cell exists (i.e., `policy` is not called when no legal move exists). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm sketching a Pentago policy using bitboards with alpha-beta search and iterative deepening, considering that the branching factor (up to 288 moves per turn) will limit search depth to around 2-3 within a 1-second budget, so I need strong move ordering and evaluation heuristics based on line counts to compensate.

Beyond immediate win detection and blocking opponent wins, I want to exploit rotation symmetry to prune duplicate positions when a quadrant is symmetric. For the board itself, I'm planning to represent it as two 36-bit integers and precompute rotation lookup tables per quadrant so I can quickly map the 9 cells to their rotated positions rather than recomputing bit extraction each time.

I'm also considering using precomputed winning-line bitmasks (32 total across rows, columns, and diagonals) so checking a win is just testing overlap against each mask. For rotations, I'm weighing whether extracting each quadrant's 9 bits one at a time is fast enough, or whether I need a smarter lookup-table extraction method since doing this naively for every move across many search nodes could get too slow in Python.

For quadrant rotation I'm designing a compact extraction using bit shifts to pull the 9 relevant bits into a 9-bit value, then using a precomputed 512-entry rotation table to get the rotated result, and finally re-expanding those bits back into place with shifts and masking — or better, precomputing a combined extraction-rotation-expansion table so a rotation becomes just one lookup plus a mask-or. I'm also thinking about whether placement and rotation can be reordered, since placing a piece outside the rotating quadrant commutes with the rotation, which could let me avoid redundant rotation computations.

Building on that, I realize for cells inside the quadrant I can precompute where each cell's bit maps to after rotation, so move generation becomes just applying 8 possible board rotations once and then a single OR operation per candidate move rather than recomputing everything from scratch. For win detection, I'm considering just checking all 32 line masks directly since that's fast enough, or alternatively using shifted-AND tricks across rows, columns, and diagonals to detect five-in-a-row without any explicit loop.

For the evaluation function, I'm counting pieces along each of the 32 possible five-in-a-row lines using popcount, scoring lines that are exclusively mine or exclusively the opponent's. But that's roughly 15 microseconds per call, and with 83k leaf nodes at depth two that balloons to over a second — too slow, so I need cheaper pruning or a lighter-weight heuristic, since vectorizing with numpy would add too much per-call overhead for single-position checks.

Given that typical arena opponents are likely simple (random or greedy), a more practical strategy is: take an immediate win if available, otherwise filter out any move that lets the opponent win on their very next reply, and among the remaining safe moves pick the best by evaluation, going deeper only if time allows. Checking all opponent replies for each of my ~288 candidate moves costs roughly 0.1-0.2 seconds, which is workable, though there's room to be smarter about which replies to check.

A cheaper trick: since placing a marble commutes with rotation, I can check whether the opponent can win in one move by testing each of the 8 possible board rotations and seeing if the resulting position has a line with four opponent marbles and one empty cell that maps back to a legal placement — this avoids brute-forcing every individual move-rotation pair.

Estimating cost: computing "at least 4 of 5 bits set" per line window using shifted bitboards takes roughly 30 bitwise ops per direction, times 4 directions times 8 rotations, landing around 1000 ops per move — noticeably faster than the naive 288-line win check, maybe a 5x speedup.

I'm now weighing whether a real depth-2 alpha-beta search is feasible. Depth 2 evaluating all 83k positions at 15µs each is too slow, but with alpha-beta pruning and decent move ordering the actual number of evaluations could drop to something like 9k, making ~150ms achievable — though depth 3 remains out of reach. I'm also considering deduplicating equivalent moves, like rotating symmetric or empty quadrants, to shrink the effective move set.

Beyond that, I want to layer in tactical shortcuts: immediate win detection, depth-2 defense against opponent winning replies, and ideally spotting depth-3 forced wins by restricting the search to moves that already create a win-in-1 threat, then checking each opponent reply cheaply. Symmetrically, I should watch for opponent double-threat moves so I can avoid walking into an unstoppable position myself.

My overall policy would proceed as: first check for an immediate winning move; then mark any move as unsafe if it lets the opponent win next turn; then check the safe moves for forced-win sequences; and finally, if none apply, fall back to a depth-2 minimax with alpha-beta pruning and move ordering by static evaluation, factoring in threats like opponent 4-in-lines.

I'm also weighing the cost of evaluating each move — scanning 32 lines per position takes roughly 13 microseconds, and full depth-2 search over all move pairs would be too slow without pruning, so I'm looking for ways to order moves and cut branches early, or precompute cheaper per-line contributions to speed up evaluation.

For the first move, I'd need to evaluate all opponent replies fully, but subsequent moves can prune early once an opponent reply drops below alpha — though this could still mean checking a large fraction of replies, roughly 29k evaluations total, which is borderline but workable with time-limited fallback to the best static move found so far. I could speed pruning by trying a cheap killer-move heuristic first — replaying whichever opponent response previously refuted a similar move, since it's likely to refute again and trigger cutoffs faster.

I also realize I can fold the win/loss safety check directly into the depth-2 search loop, exiting immediately when the opponent has a winning reply, and this pre-filtering keeps costs manageable at roughly 23ms across all moves. For tactical forced wins, I'd check whether any of my safe moves creates an immediate winning threat, then verify across all opponent replies whether that threat survives — handling edge cases where my winning move might also hand the opponent five-in-a-row, which I treat as not a win.

I confirm that any four-in-a-row-plus-gap threat is always completable, since a length-5 line only ever spans at most 2-3 quadrants, guaranteeing a free quadrant to rotate without disrupting the winning line — so open fours are essentially forced wins for whoever is about to move. This means my evaluation function should assign huge value to my open fours after the opponent's reply (since it'd be my move next), while treating the opponent's open fours as dangerous-but-blockable rather than immediately losing, and I'll skip the more expensive recursive threat-detection at eval leaves to save time, relying instead on line-based weight penalties.

I'm setting a real-machine time budget of roughly half a second with frequent time checks, and now moving into implementation: defining quadrant cell groups, precomputing rotation destination maps for clockwise and counterclockwise rotations, and building a bitboard rotation function via lookup tables that extracts a quadrant's 9 bits, remaps them, and reinserts them into the full board efficiently.

Writing move generation and dedup logic...

I'm reasoning through a subtle deduplication case — quadrants that are rotationally symmetric produce the same rotated board for both left and right turns, but placing a new piece in an empty symmetric quadrant can still land in different final cells depending on rotation direction, so I can only skip the redundant direction when checking sets of reachable positions overall, not per individual placement.
